Lessons.Title: Generate Equivalent Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 warm-up Number Talk Something Times 8 has FOUR mental calculations: 2×8=16;6×8=48;10×8=80;12×8=96. Explain using related products, e.g. 12×8=10×8+2×8.

Source Activity1 Show Equivalence first displays a rectangle divided into four equal areas, two shaded. Jada asserts the shaded area also represents 4/8. Jada is right: divide EACH of the four quarters into two equal pieces without changing the whole or shaded area. 2/4=4/8. Tyler's concern invites a student-made diagram and explanation, not just the correct number.

Source Activity1 then requires three exact additional proofs: 1/3=2/6,6/8=3/4,6/6=2/2, each from their original 2021 drawn representations. Equal subdivisions may be regrouped but SAME whole and SAME shaded area must remain. Original drawings were read on Our-CS; independently drawn Edulytics teaching replaces copyrighted pixels.

Source Activity2 More Than One Name includes three original student diagrams: four of six equal pieces shaded =>4/6=2/3; two of eight equal pieces shaded =>2/8=1/4; four of four equal pieces shaded =>4/4=2/2=1. The source asks students to supply TWO valid names (additional equivalent names are allowed with correct reasoning).

The last source diagram is crucial: TWO equal-size whole rectangles, EACH split in half, together four half-sized regions but THREE shaded. Thus three half-sized parts from the same whole measure 3/2=6/4=1+1/2, NOT 3/4. There are two wholes, so treating the four visible half pieces as one whole gives a wrong denominator. Count equal unit fractions per ONE whole, not total pieces across both figures.

Source lesson synthesis asks pupils to show how shaded same-whole regions can have different fraction names, and a teacher checks drawings and explanations. Source teacher-gated Cool-down Two Fraction Names for Each Diagram was not accessed or reproduced. Original standalone student PDF, tests and Stage D are unverified.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fraction by subdividing
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide each of a whole's equal parts into the same count of smaller equal parts without changing shaded amount.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number fraction names
KeyConcepts.Definition: When all parts of one equal whole are shaded, the represented value is 1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple unit wholes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Denominator counts equal-sized parts per each unit whole; several wholes may show an improper fraction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Three parts each one half of ONE whole count as 3/2, even if two whole figures are drawn.
KeyConcepts.Example: The source last image is 3/2=6/4, not 3/4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Number Talk all source products
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute 2×8,6×8,10×8,12×8 mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply by eight using related known products.

WorkedExamples.Title: Jada first rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Two of four equal cells are shaded. Show why 4/8 is also correct.
WorkedExamples.Method: Split every original fourth in half.
Steps: Four eighths are shaded after new equal subdivisions.
Area and unit whole remain unchanged.

WorkedExamples.Title: One third to sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Repartition one of three equal parts into sixths.
WorkedExamples.Method: Split each third into two equal pieces.
Steps: One third shaded in a three-part whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Six eighths to fourths
WorkedExamples.Question: Use the original six-of-eight shading to show fourths.
Steps: Six of eight equal regions are shaded.
Pair each two eighths into a fourth.

WorkedExamples.Title: Other original three rectangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Name equivalences for 4/6, 2/8, 4/4 shaded.
WorkedExamples.Method: Regroup congruent parts of one whole.
Steps: Four sixths group to two thirds.
Two eighths group to one fourth.
Four fourths of the whole equal two halves.
WorkedExamples.Check: All equivalent names preserve each whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original two-whole improper fraction
WorkedExamples.Question: Two equal whole rectangles, each divided into halves, have three of four regions shaded.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count half-sized units across BOTH separate whole figures.
Steps: Each original rectangle separately represents 1 whole.
Each contains two half-sized regions; three half-regions shaded total.
WorkedExamples.Check: More than one complete whole is shaded.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Label final three shaded parts as 3/4 because four visible regions are present.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The regions belong to TWO complete whole rectangles, not a single fourth-partitioned whole.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reject Jada's 4/8 because the original has only four drawn regions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Dividing each fourth in half changes the number of pieces but not shaded amount.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw the added equal partitions to verify.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Infer diagram equivalence solely from a typed scalar ratio.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Shading and same-whole visual geometry remain unverified by a number.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks equal area and partition reasoning.

SummaryPoints: Activity2:4/6=2/3,2/8=1/4,4/4=2/2; last two-whole image is 3/2=6/4, NOT 3/4.
Teacher checks source-equivalent diagrams and whole-size consistency; original gated Cool-down and standalone student PDF unverified; tests/Stage D deferred.
